title: New mechanical forces modify many correlated parts together, not isolated bones

fields.label: Label
fields.value: New mechanical forces modify many correlated parts together, not isolated bones

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When altered environment and habits introduce new forces, the resulting modifications of form appear not as isolated changes in single parts but as slow, general, graded modifications spread over many correlated parts or the whole body.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And if this be really so, it will further imply that modifications of form will tend to manifest themselves, not so much in small and _isolated_ phenomena, in this part of the fabric or in that, in a scapula for instance or a humerus: but rather in some slow, _general_, and more or less uniform or graded modification, spread over a number of correlated parts

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Mechanics and phylogeny”. Scope: evolutionary change of form in animals, especially skeletons

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Coordinated change is measurable, and multivariate public morphology is substantial. Existing observational data cannot cleanly attribute covariance to mechanical forces rather than development, selection or phylogeny.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify whether ecological transitions and altered mechanical regimes are associated with coordinated, graded changes across multiple anatomical modules rather than isolated traits, using phylogenetic multivariate models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Shared development and ancestry also generate trait covariance.

“New forces” and “isolated” require arbitrary definitions.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Integration of shape across skeletal parts is a standard analysis on open scans and trees. The claim adds that new mechanical forces are what produce the graded pattern, and integration studies also match developmental correlation. Current data can document coordinated change and cannot isolate the mechanical cause.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: After habitat or locomotor shifts, measure whether shape change is spread in a graded way across many skeletal regions or concentrated in single bones. Support would be higher morphological integration and more spatially graded change in those transitions than in single-element outliers; a record of isolated, bone-by-bone changes would refute the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Fossil sequences rarely preserve enough associated elements to separate graded change from sampling gaps.

Developmental pleiotropy produces correlated change whether or not new mechanical forces are the cause.
